summary: Surveys and classifies the mechanisms in IETF transport protocols such as TCP, MPTCP, SCTP, UDP, UDP-Lite and DCCP, as background for defining common transport services.

eli5.summary: A catalog of what each way of sending data over the internet can do, so you can compare.

questions: tcp vs udp which to use
subtitle: Comparing what different ways of sending data over the Internet can do

tldr.problem: Applications need different delivery guarantees, latency tolerances, and functionality from transport protocols, but understanding which protocol provides which service is difficult.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF has defined various transport protocols (TCP, UDP, SCTP, MPTCP, DCCP, UDP-Lite) and related technologies (RTP, OWAMP, TWAMP, TLS, HTTP) that provide different combinations of features like reliability, ordering, flow control, congestion control, and security.
tldr.outcome: Developers and operators now have a documented taxonomy of transport services including connection-oriented and connectionless delivery, unicast and multicast, stream and datagram modes, and varying levels of reliability and security, enabling informed protocol selection.

today: RFC 8095 remains current as a comprehensive survey of IETF transport protocols. These protocols continue to form the foundation of Internet transport services, with TCP and UDP remaining dominant while SCTP, MPTCP, and DCCP serve specialized use cases. Modern applications increasingly use TLS/DTLS for security and HTTP/WebSockets for compatibility with network infrastructure.

sections.title: Transport Services and Protocol Landscape
sections.content:
A transport service is the end-to-end service provided to an application by the transport layer. Applications need different services: some require reliable in-order delivery, others prioritize low latency and can tolerate occasional loss. Transport features include reliability, ordering, message boundaries, flow control, congestion control, and security. The service an application needs depends on its requirements, which may be determined at design time, compile time, or runtime.

Beyond TCP and UDP, the IETF has standardized SCTP (multi-stream ordered delivery), DCCP (datagram congestion control), MPTCP (multi-path TCP), and UDP-Lite (partial integrity protection). Additionally, services may be layered on top of these: TLS/DTLS adds security, HTTP runs over TCP, RTP carries real-time media, and WebRTC uses multiple protocols together. Each combination offers different guarantees about delivery, latency, and functionality.

This document surveys the mechanisms provided by existing IETF protocols as background for defining a common set of transport services. Understanding the landscape enables better protocol design and application development decisions.
sections.eli5: Different applications need different kinds of service. A phone call needs fast delivery but doesn't need everything. A file download needs everything to arrive but doesn't mind waiting. This document explains what each protocol does.

sections.title: Reliable Connection-Oriented Transport
sections.content:
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the default connection-oriented, stream-based transport. It provides a three-way handshake for connection setup and feature negotiation, and orderly completion or immediate teardown of connections. TCP partitions a continuous byte stream into segments, using sequence numbers to order segments on receipt and detect loss. Reliable delivery is implemented through acknowledgments; the receiver confirms delivery, and missing segments are retransmitted using either a retransmission timer with exponential backoff or detection of duplicate acknowledgments.

TCP includes flow control using a sliding window mechanism that limits outstanding data, and congestion control through a congestion window managed by algorithms like slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery. Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) allows networks to signal congestion without inducing loss. TCP also provides optional Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) for faster identification of missing segments. All data is transmitted as unicast only.

MPTCP (Multipath TCP) extends TCP to support multihoming for resilience, mobility, and load balancing. It multiplexes a single byte stream over multiple TCP subflows between different IP address pairs (IPv4 and IPv6). This enables soft failover when one path fails and throughput aggregation across multiple paths using either coupled or uncoupled congestion control.

SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) provides message-based delivery with multiple independent streams. Unlike TCP's single stream, SCTP supports multiple ordered streams simultaneously, enabling head-of-line blocking prevention: loss in one stream does not delay delivery in others. SCTP provides full or partial reliability options and supports multihoming. A four-way handshake establishes associations, and SCTP includes built-in heartbeat mechanisms and error handling.
sections.eli5: TCP is like a phone call: you establish a connection, everything arrives in order, and the other person confirms they got everything. SCTP is like multiple phone lines so one broken line doesn't stop other conversations. MPTCP is like using multiple internet connections at once.

sections.title: Datagram and Connectionless Services
sections.content:
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and maintains message boundaries. It provides no error correction, congestion control, or flow control, allowing applications to send messages independently without setup. UDP supports unicast, multicast, and broadcast transmission and is widely used for DNS, video streaming, and online gaming. Applications using UDP must implement their own congestion control (such as NewReno, TFRC, or LEDBAT) if they need it.

UDP-Lite extends UDP by allowing applications to specify partial integrity protection: only the first part of a packet (the header and critical payload portions) is protected by checksum, while the remainder is exempt. This enables corruption-tolerant applications like video and audio streaming to accept damaged packets rather than requiring retransmission of entire messages.

DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) combines datagram messaging with congestion control. DCCP provides partial reliability (allowing some messages to be dropped) and framing similar to UDP, but includes congestion control mechanisms for applications sensitive to congestion but not requiring full reliability. This makes DCCP suitable for interactive applications like VoIP where timely delivery matters more than complete delivery.
sections.eli5: UDP is like yelling across a crowd: quick, but you're not sure everyone hears you. UDP-Lite lets you send damaged video if it's fast enough. DCCP is like shouting politely: it backs off when the crowd is loud, but doesn't wait for confirmation that everyone heard.

sections.title: Security and Specialized Transport
sections.content:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) and DTLS (Datagram TLS) are pseudotransports providing confidentiality, integrity, and authentication over TCP (TLS) or UDP (DTLS). They operate at the presentation layer but provide features often associated with transport services. TLS runs record-based sessions with connection setup and negotiation, while DTLS provides similar security over unreliable datagrams. Both use symmetric encryption for data and asymmetric cryptography for key exchange and authentication.

RTP (Real-Time Transport Protocol) is a framework for real-time media delivery, typically over UDP. It adds sequence numbers, timestamps, and synchronization source identification to support time-sensitive applications like voice and video. RTP enables receivers to detect out-of-order or missing packets and provides timing information for proper playback. Congestion control and reliability mechanisms are left to the application or upper-layer protocol.

HTTP as a pseudotransport (HTTP/1.1 over TCP or HTTP/2 over TCP) provides message multiplexing, request/response semantics, and optional compression. Applications can tunnel protocols through HTTP for compatibility with firewalls and proxies. WebSockets over HTTP enable bidirectional, low-latency communication.

Multicast transport protocols like FLUTE/ALC and NORM provide reliable multicast delivery for distributing files or streams to many receivers simultaneously. FLUTE/ALC uses Forward Error Correction for loss recovery; NORM uses negative acknowledgments (NACK) to request retransmission of lost packets.
sections.eli5: TLS adds encryption to TCP or UDP so nobody can read your data. RTP carries video and audio with timestamps so they play smoothly. HTTP can carry almost anything if normal connections don't work. Multicast lets you send the same data to many people at once.

sections.title: Transport Features and Protocol Selection
sections.content:
Transport features differentiate protocols and enable protocol selection. Connection model features include connection-oriented (TCP, SCTP) versus connectionless (UDP, DCCP). Addressing features include unicast (one-to-one), anycast (to one of many), and multicast (to many simultaneously). Stream vs. datagram framing determines whether data is treated as continuous bytes or discrete messages.

Reliability features vary: TCP provides full reliability with retransmission; SCTP offers full or partial reliability; DCCP provides congestion control without reliability; UDP-Lite allows partial integrity protection. Ordering features differ: TCP and SCTP provide ordered delivery, but SCTP allows unordered delivery within streams; UDP and DCCP do not guarantee order.

Flow control features limit sender rates: TCP and SCTP use window-based mechanisms; UDP has none. Congestion control is mandatory for TCP and SCTP, optional for UDP (left to application), and built into DCCP. Security features like confidentiality and integrity are typically provided by TLS/DTLS rather than transport protocols themselves.

Protocol selection should consider application requirements, network constraints, and deployment scenarios. Real-time applications might choose UDP with application-layer recovery and congestion control. File transfer needs TCP's reliability. Video streaming might use RTP over UDP with application-level error correction. The diversity of IETF transport protocols and services supports a wide range of application requirements.
sections.eli5: Each protocol is good for different things: TCP for anything important, UDP for speed, SCTP for multiple messages, DCCP for real-time, TLS for secrecy. Pick based on what your application needs.
